blocks: Starting lineups are set on the league website. Each player locks at the kickoff of his own NFL game: until then an owner may move him into or out of the starting lineup, and after it he stays where he is. Players not in the starting lineup at their kickoff do not score for the team.
The website always uses the last lineup saved, so an owner may change his starting lineup as often as he likes before each player's kickoff.

ops.find: If an owner fails to submit a starting lineup by the deadline, then the previous week's lineup will serve as the default-starting lineup.
ops.to: If an owner does not submit a starting lineup, the previous week's lineup serves as the default starting lineup, and the owner may still change any player in it before that player's kickoff.

ops.find: superstar level shall cost three retainment slots.
blocks: Players tied for a level all belong to the higher level, so a level can hold more players than its count. If the third and fourth RBs finish with the same points, for example, both are superstars.

ops.find: No transactions will be allowed beginning the last week of the NFL regular season and continuing through to the day of the NFL Pro Bowl game. The day after the Pro Bowl game is the first day that trades may be made.
ops.to: No trades are allowed from the trade deadline (section 7.1) until the PDL Super Bowl is over. The day after the Super Bowl is the first day that trades may be made.

blocks: Players are placed on waivers to give every owner an equal chance to acquire them. After the draft, any player not on a roster is on waivers, and so is any player a team drops.

Waiver claims are processed once a week by the league website, on Thursday morning. If only one team claims a player, that team gets him. If two or more teams claim the same player, the team with the higher waiver priority gets him. An owner who claims more than one player ranks his claims, and they are awarded in that order.
Waiver priority is a season-long rolling order. It starts in draft order, and a team whose claim succeeds drops to the bottom of the list.

After waivers are processed, every player not just dropped is a free agent, first come first served, until his game kicks off, and signing a free agent does not affect waiver priority. A player dropped in the waiver run stays on waivers until the next week's run. A free agent not signed by his kickoff goes back on waivers.

blocks: Each team has one injured reserve spot during the regular season. A player in it must carry an official NFL designation: injured reserve, injured reserve designated to return, physically unable to perform, or non-football injury. The team must make room for him on the roster the moment he is eligible to return.

ops.find: The league champion takes home 75% of the rest and the runner up receives 25%.
ops.to: Of the rest, the league champion takes home 67%, the runner up 20%, third place 6.5%, and the team scoring the most regular-season points 6.5%.

mfl_known_differences.why: MFL's 2006 and 2007 yardage rules are in an older encoding, with overlapping ranges (50 and up at '0/0' alongside 100 and up at 1 per 10), that cannot be read as the book's bonus table. From 2008 MFL spells the tiers out, and they match the book: 5 points at 50 yards, 10 at 100, and 5 for a QB at 200 passing yards.
